column2: From Tamīm al-Dārī (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The religion is sincere counsel (naṣīḥah)” — three times. We said: To whom, O Messenger of Allah?
He said: “To Allah, to His Book, to His Messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims and to their common people.” Reported by Muslim.

Muslim recorded this hadith in the narration of Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yazīd al-Laythī, from Tamīm al-Dārī. It has also been narrated from Suhayl and others, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayrah,

from the Prophet ﷺ, and al-Tirmidhī recorded it by this route. Some scholars held it authentic by both routes together, while others said that the authentic one is the hadith of Tamīm and that the other chain is a mistake.
This hadith has also been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ in the hadiths of Ibn ʿUmar, Thawbān, Ibn ʿAbbās and others.
We mentioned at the beginning of the book that Abū Dāwūd said this hadith is one of the hadiths around which jurisprudence revolves.
The ḥāfiẓ Abū Nuʿaym said: This is a hadith of great importance; Muḥammad ibn Aslam al-Ṭūsī mentioned that it is one quarter of the religion.

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded from the hadith of Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever does not concern himself with the affairs of the Muslims is not one of them; and whoever does not spend his evening and his morning sincere towards Allah, His Messenger, His Book, his leader and the common Muslims is not one of them.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded from the hadith of Abū Umāmah that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: The dearest way in which My servant worships Me is by being sincere towards Me.”

Many hadiths speak of sincere counsel to the Muslims in general; some speak of sincere counsel to those in authority over them, and some of the sincere counsel owed by those in authority to their subjects.

As for the first, sincere counsel to the Muslims in general: in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Jarīr ibn ʿAbdullāh said: I pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ on establishing the prayer, paying zakāh and giving sincere counsel to every Muslim.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The believer has six rights over the believer,” and among them he mentioned: “When he asks you for counsel, give him sincere counsel.”
This hadith has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by other routes as well.
In the Musnad, from Ḥakīm ibn Abī Yazīd, from his father, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“When one of you asks his brother for counsel, let him give him sincere counsel.”
As for the second, sincere counsel to those in authority and their sincere counsel to their subjects: in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Allah is pleased with three things for you: He is pleased for you to worship Him and not associate anything with Him, to hold fast all together to the rope of Allah and not be divided, and to give sincere counsel to those whom Allah has put in charge of your affairs.”

In the Musnad and elsewhere, from Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim, the Prophet ﷺ said in his sermon at al-Khayf in Minā: “There are three things against which the heart of a Muslim harbours no rancour: doing deeds sincerely for Allah, giving sincere counsel to those in authority, and keeping to the main body (jamāʿah) of the Muslims.”
This sermon was narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by a number of Companions, among them Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī.

The hadith of Abū Saʿīd has also been narrated in other wording, which al-Dāraquṭnī recorded in al-Afrād with a good chain. Its wording is that the Prophet ﷺ said: “There are three things against which the heart of a Muslim harbours no rancour: sincere counsel to Allah, to His Messenger, to His Book and to the common Muslims.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Maʿqil ibn Yasār, the Prophet ﷺ said: “There is no servant whom Allah entrusts with a flock and who then does not guard it with sincere counsel, but he will not enter Paradise.”
Allah has mentioned in His Book that the prophets (peace be upon them) gave sincere counsel to their nations, as He related of Nūḥ and of Ṣāliḥ.
The Exalted said: “There is no blame on the weak, nor on the sick, nor on those who find nothing to spend, if they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger” [al-Tawbah 9:91]. That is,

whoever stays behind from jihād for a valid excuse is not to blame, provided that he is sincere to Allah and His Messenger in staying behind; for the hypocrites used to put forward false excuses and stayed behind from jihād without being sincere to Allah and His Messenger.
The Prophet ﷺ said that the religion is sincere counsel. This shows that sincere counsel covers the qualities of Islam, faith and excellence (iḥsān) mentioned in the hadith of Jibrīl,
all of which he called religion. For sincerity towards Allah requires carrying out what He has made obligatory in the most complete way,

which is the station of iḥsān; sincerity towards Allah is not complete without it. That cannot be achieved without complete love, both the obligatory and the recommended, and it entails striving to draw near to Him through voluntary acts of obedience in this same way, and leaving forbidden and disliked things in this same way too.
Among the mursal reports of al-Ḥasan, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Tell me, if one of you had two slaves, one of whom obeyed him when he gave him an order,

returned what he was entrusted with, and was true to him when he was away, while the other disobeyed him when he gave him an order, betrayed him when he entrusted him with something and cheated him when he was away — would they be equal?”
They said: No. He said: “That is how you are with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.” Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it.
Imam Aḥmad recorded something with the same meaning from the hadith of Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ.
Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: Love is better than fear. Do you not see that if you had two slaves, one of whom loved you and the other feared you,

the one who loves you would be true to you whether you were present or absent, because he loves you, while the one who fears you might be true to you when you are present, because he is afraid, but cheat you and not be true to you when you are absent?
ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rufayʿ said: The disciples said to ʿĪsā (peace be upon him): What deed is truly sincere?
He said: One for which you do not love people to praise you. They said: And what is sincerity towards Allah?

He said: That you put Allah's right before the right of people; and if two matters present themselves to you, one for Allah and the other for this world, you begin with the right of Allah the Exalted.

Al-Khaṭṭābī said: Naṣīḥah is a word that expresses a whole complex of meaning, namely wanting good for the one counselled. He said: The root meaning of nuṣḥ in the language is purity; one says naṣaḥtu al-ʿasal when one has cleared honey of its wax.

So the meaning of sincerity towards Allah, Glorified is He, is sound belief in His oneness and sincere intention in worshipping Him; sincerity towards His Book is believing in it and acting on what it contains; sincerity towards His Messenger is affirming his prophethood and devoting obedience to him in what he commanded and forbade; and sincere counsel to the common Muslims is guiding them to what is in their interest. End of quotation.

Imam Abū ʿAbdillāh Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī, in his book Taʿẓīm Qadr al-Ṣalāh, reported from one of the people of knowledge an explanation of this hadith that could not be bettered, and we relate it here in his own words.
Muḥammad ibn Naṣr said: One of the people of knowledge said: The sum of the explanation of naṣīḥah is the heart's concern for the one counselled, whoever he may be. It is of two kinds,

one obligatory and the other supererogatory. Obligatory sincerity towards Allah is the sincere person's intense concern to follow the love of Allah in carrying out what He has made obligatory and keeping away from what He has forbidden.
Supererogatory sincerity is preferring His love to love of oneself. That is, when two matters present themselves, one for oneself and the other for one's Lord, one begins with what is for one's Lord

and puts off what is for oneself. This is the summary explanation of sincerity towards Allah, both its obligatory and its supererogatory parts. It has a detailed explanation, part of which we shall give so that whoever does not grasp the summary may grasp it through the details.

Its obligatory part is keeping away from what He forbids and carrying out what He has made obligatory with all one's limbs, as far as one is able. If one is unable to carry out His obligations because of some affliction that has befallen one, such as illness,
imprisonment or the like, one resolves to carry out what has been made obligatory as soon as the cause that prevents one is removed.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “There is no blame on the weak, nor on the sick, nor on those who find nothing to spend, if they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger; there is no way [of blame] against those who do good” [al-Tawbah 9:91]. He called them doers of good (muḥsinūn) because of their sincerity towards Allah in their hearts when they were prevented from going out to jihād in person.

All deeds may be lifted from the servant in some situations, but sincerity towards Allah is never lifted from him. Were he so ill that he could do nothing with any of his limbs, tongue or otherwise, while his mind remained sound,

sincerity towards Allah in his heart would still not be lifted from him: that he regret his sins and intend, if he recovers, to carry out what Allah has made obligatory on him and avoid what He has forbidden him. Otherwise he would not be sincere towards Allah in his heart.

The same applies to sincerity towards Allah and towards His Messenger ﷺ in what he made obligatory on people by his Lord's command. Part of obligatory sincerity towards Allah is not being content with the sin of the sinner, and loving the obedience of whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger.

Supererogatory sincerity, which is not obligatory, is exerting every effort to prefer Allah the Exalted over everything one loves, with the heart and all the limbs, until the sincere person has nothing left over for anything else.

For when someone who is sincere to another strives his utmost, he does not prefer himself over him, and he does everything that would bring the other joy and that the other loves; and so it is with the one who is sincere towards his Lord. Whoever performs voluntary acts for Allah without striving his utmost is sincere in proportion to his deeds, but does not merit sincerity in its completeness.

Sincerity towards the Book of Allah is intense love for it and reverence for its standing, since it is the speech of the Creator; an intense desire to understand it; and intense concern to reflect on it and to pause over it when reciting it,

in search of the meanings that his Master loves him to understand from Him, and then to act on them for Him once he has understood them. In the same way a sincere servant among men understands the instructions of the one he is sincere to,
and if a letter comes to him from him, he takes care to understand it so as to carry out what he has written to him in it. So too the one sincere towards his Lord's Book takes care to understand it,

so as to carry out for Allah what He has commanded, as He loves and is pleased with. Then he spreads what he has understood among people and keeps studying it constantly, out of love for it, taking on its character and adopting its manners.
Sincerity towards the Messenger ﷺ in his lifetime was exerting every effort in obeying him, supporting him and helping him, giving wealth when he wanted it, and hastening to what he loved.

After his death, it is concern to seek out his Sunnah, to inquire into his character and manners, to revere his command and hold to carrying it out; intense anger at, and turning away from, anyone who takes as his religion what goes against his Sunnah; anger at anyone who neglects it for some worldly advantage,

even if he holds to it as religion; love for anyone connected with him by kinship, marriage, emigration, support, or companionship in Islam for an hour of a night or a day; and resembling him in his appearance and his dress.

Sincerity towards the leaders of the Muslims is loving their uprightness, their right guidance and their justice; loving that the Ummah should unite under them and hating that it should split over them; holding obedience to them in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as part of one's religion; hating anyone who thinks of rebelling against them; and loving that they be strengthened in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Sincerity towards the Muslims is loving for them what one loves for oneself and hating for them what one hates for oneself; being tender towards them, merciful to their young and respectful to their old; grieving at their grief and rejoicing at their joy, even if that harms one's own worldly interests — as when their prices fall,

even if that means losing the profit on what one sells in one's trade — and likewise with everything that harms them in general; and loving their wellbeing, their harmony, the continuance of blessings upon them, their victory over their enemy, and the warding off of every harm and hardship from them.
Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Ṣalāḥ said: Naṣīḥah is a comprehensive word that includes the one giving sincere counsel doing every kind of good for the one he counsels, in will and in deed.

Sincerity towards Allah the Exalted is affirming His oneness, describing Him with attributes of perfection and majesty, and declaring Him free of whatever opposes and contradicts them; avoiding disobedience to Him; carrying out obedience to Him and what He loves, with sincerity; loving for His sake and hating for His sake; striving against those who disbelieve in Him, the Exalted, and the like; and calling people to that and urging them to it.

Sincerity towards His Book is believing in it, revering it and keeping it free [of distortion]; reciting it as it should be recited; standing by its commands and prohibitions; seeking to understand its sciences and its parables; reflecting on its verses; calling people to it; and defending it against the distortions of extremists and the attacks of heretics.

Sincerity towards His Messenger is close to that: believing in him and in what he brought; honouring and revering him; holding fast to obedience to him; reviving his Sunnah, seeking out his knowledge and spreading it; showing enmity to whoever is hostile to him and to it, and loyalty to whoever is loyal to him and to it; taking on his character and adopting his manners; loving his family and his Companions; and the like.

Sincerity towards the leaders of the Muslims is helping them in what is right, obeying them in it, reminding them of it and alerting them gently and courteously; refraining from rising up against them; praying for them to be granted success; and urging others to do so.

Sincere counsel to the common Muslims is guiding them to what is in their interest, teaching them the affairs of their religion and their worldly life, covering their faults, meeting their needs, helping them against their enemies, defending them,
avoiding cheating and envying them, loving for them what one loves for oneself and hating for them what one hates for oneself, and the like. End of what he said.

Among the kinds of sincere counsel to them that consist in warding off harm and hardship from them are preferring their poor to oneself, teaching their ignorant, and turning back those of them who stray from the truth in word or deed by bringing them back to it gently,
and being kind to them in commanding right and forbidding wrong, out of love to remove their corruption, even if it costs one some harm in one's worldly life.
As one of the Salaf said: I wish that these people obeyed Allah, even if my flesh were cut to pieces with shears. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to say:

If only I could act among you according to the Book of Allah and you acted by it! Every time I put a Sunnah into practice among you, a limb of mine would fall away, until the last of it was my soul leaving me.

Among the kinds of sincerity towards Allah the Exalted, His Book and His Messenger — one that belongs particularly to scholars — is refuting the misguiding heresies (ahwāʾ) with the Book and the Sunnah,
and showing how both of them point against all such heresies; likewise refuting weak views that are slips of scholars, and showing how the Book and the Sunnah point to their refutation.

Part of this is showing which hadiths of the Prophet ﷺ are authentic and which are not, by making clear the state of their narrators — whose narrations are accepted and whose are not — and showing the mistakes made by those reliable narrators whose narration is accepted.
One of the greatest kinds of sincere counsel is to counsel sincerely whoever consults you about his affairs, as he ﷺ said:

“When one of you asks his brother for counsel, let him give him sincere counsel.” In some hadiths: “Part of the right of a Muslim over a Muslim is that he be true to him in his absence.” This means that if he is spoken ill of in his absence, he should support him

and defend him; and if he sees someone who wants to harm him in his absence, he should restrain him. Being true to someone in his absence shows the truthfulness of one's sincerity, for a person may show sincerity in someone's presence out of flattery and cheat him in his absence.
Al-Ḥasan said: You will not fulfil the due of your sincere counsel to your brother until you command him to do what you yourself fall short of.

Al-Ḥasan said: One of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said: By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you wish I will swear to you by Allah that the most beloved of Allah's servants to Allah are those who make Allah beloved to His servants and make Allah's servants beloved to Allah, and who go about the earth with sincere counsel.

Farqad al-Sabakhī said: I read in one of the scriptures: The one who loves Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is a commander set over the commanders; his throng will be the first of the throngs on the Day of Resurrection, and his seat the nearest of the seats there. Love is the utmost of nearness and striving, and those who love will never weary of long striving for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

They love Him and love to remember Him, and make Him beloved to His creation; they walk among His servants with sincere counsel, and fear for them because of their deeds on the Day when scandals are laid bare. They are the friends of Allah, His beloved ones and His chosen elite; they are the ones who will have no rest until they meet Him.
Ibn ʿUlayyah said concerning the words of Abū Bakr al-Muzanī — “Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) did not surpass the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by fasting or prayer,
but by something that was in his heart” — he said: What was in his heart was love for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and sincere counsel towards His creation.

Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: Those among us who reached the rank they reached did not reach it through much prayer and fasting; among us, they reached it through generosity of soul, soundness of heart and sincere counsel to the Ummah.
Ibn al-Mubārak was asked: Which deeds are best?
He said: Sincerity towards Allah.
Maʿmar said: It used to be said: The most sincere of people towards you is the one who fears Allah regarding you.

When the Salaf wanted to give someone sincere counsel, they admonished him in private, so much so that one of them said: Whoever admonishes his brother privately, between the two of them, has given sincere counsel; whoever admonishes him in front of people has only rebuked him.
Al-Fuḍayl said: The believer conceals and counsels; the wicked man exposes and reviles.

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Rawwād said: Among those before you, when a man saw something in his brother, he would counsel him gently, and he would be rewarded for his commanding and forbidding. But one of these people now deals harshly with his companion, provokes his brother's anger and tears away his cover.
Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) was asked about commanding the ruler to do right and forbidding him from wrong. He said: If you must do it, then let it be between you and him.
Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: A Muslim is not obliged to give sincere counsel to a dhimmī, but he is obliged to give it to a Muslim.
The Prophet ﷺ said: “…and sincere counsel to every Muslim, and that he give sincere counsel to the community of the Muslims and their common people.”
